title: Use Our Salary After Tax Calculator to Convert Hourly Rates to Annual Pay
description: Convert your hourly rate to annual salary with our salary after tax calculator. Includes 38-hour week, fortnightly pay, tax estimates, and superannuation for 2026–27.
salarySummary: For a full-time employee working 38 hours per week, annual gross pay is hourly rate × 38 × 52, and our salary after tax calculator estimates the after-tax and super amounts.

faqs.q: How do I use the salary after tax calculator to convert my hourly rate?
faqs.a: Enter your base hourly rate into the timesheet on our home page. If you are a casual employee, check the 25% casual loading box – do not add loading to your rate beforehand. The calculator then multiplies by 38 hours per week and 52 weeks to give annual gross pay, then deducts estimated tax (using 2026–27 resident rates and Medicare levy) and adds 12% superannuation on top of ordinary earnings.

faqs.q: Does the salary after tax calculator include superannuation in the annual figure?
faqs.a: No. Superannuation is shown separately as an amount paid on top of your ordinary earnings. The calculator uses 12% of your gross ordinary earnings, up to the $270,830 maximum contribution base. The annual salary figure is your gross pay before super, and the after-tax amount is what you receive in hand.

faqs.q: What if I work more or fewer than 38 hours per week?
faqs.a: The calculator assumes a standard 38-hour week for full-time employees. If your hours differ, you can adjust the weekly hours in the timesheet. The formula remains hourly rate × hours per week × 52. For part-time or casual workers, the same method applies using your actual weekly hours.

bodyMarkdown:
## Convert Your Hourly Rate to Annual Pay with Our Salary After Tax Calculator

Understanding your annual salary from an hourly rate is essential whether you are negotiating a job offer, comparing pay rates, or planning your budget. Our [salary after tax calculator](/topics/take-home) does the heavy lifting: it converts your hourly pay into annual gross income, estimates tax and Medicare, and shows superannuation on top. All figures use the latest Fair Work and ATO benchmarks for 2026–27.

### The Basic Formula: Hourly × Hours × 52

Annual gross pay = hourly rate × hours worked per week × 52 weeks. For a full-time employee, we assume 38 hours per week – the standard under the Fair Work Act. If you work a different number of hours, simply enter your usual weekly hours into the timesheet. The calculator also shows your fortnightly pay (weekly pay × 2), which is useful for budgeting between pay cycles.

### What the Calculator Includes

- **Gross annual salary** – your hourly rate multiplied by weekly hours and 52 weeks.
- **Estimated tax** – using the 2026–27 resident tax rates: nil up to $18,200; 15% from $18,201 to $45,000; 30% from $45,001 to $135,000; 37% from $135,001 to $190,000; 45% above $190,000. The calculator also applies the Medicare levy at 2% (using the 2025–26 single reduction thresholds as 2026–27 thresholds were not confirmed).
- **Superannuation** – 12% of your ordinary earnings, paid on top of your salary, up to the $270,830 maximum contribution base. Super is not deducted from your pay; it is an employer contribution.
- **Casual loading** – if you are a casual employee, check the 25% loading box. The calculator adds 25% to your base rate before computing annual figures. Never enter a rate that already includes casual loading.

### Understanding Ordinary-Time Earnings

The Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) publishes Average Weekly Earnings (AWE) data. For May 2026, full-time adult ordinary-time earnings were $2,083.70 per week. That figure represents the average weekly pay for full-time employees before tax, including overtime and bonuses. By contrast, all employees total earnings (including part-time workers) averaged $1,579.20 per week. These averages are not medians for any specific job – they are broader industry and state averages. Our [reference tables](/data) provide more detail on how these figures compare.

### Minimum Wage and Award Rates

The National Minimum Wage from 1 July 2026 is $26.44 per hour, or $1,004.90 per week for 38 hours. Casual employees receive a 25% loading, bringing the casual minimum to $33.05 per hour. Many employees are covered by awards that set higher minimum rates. Use our [pay guides](/blog) to check the correct award rate for your industry. The calculator works with any hourly rate you enter, but always ensure you are being paid at least the minimum applicable to your job.

### Tax and Super: What You Actually Take Home

After tax and Medicare, your take-home pay is what lands in your bank account. Our [salary after tax calculator](/topics/take-home) estimates this amount. For example, a full-time employee earning the national minimum wage of $26.44 per hour would have a gross annual salary of about $52,265 (38 hours × 52 weeks). After tax and Medicare, the estimated annual take-home pay would be approximately $42,600 (depending on individual circumstances). Superannuation of 12% ($6,272) is paid on top by the employer.

### Fortnightly and Weekly Breakdown

If you are paid fortnightly, multiply your weekly pay by two. For the minimum wage example, weekly gross is $1,004.90, so fortnightly gross is $2,009.80. After tax, the fortnightly take-home would be roughly $1,638. The calculator shows these figures automatically.

### Important Notes and Limitations

Annual pay here is hourly rate × hours per week × 52. It assumes the same rate every week, no unpaid overtime, no penalty rates, no allowances, and no salary sacrifice. Super is estimated at 12% of ordinary earnings only, paid on top, and stops at the $270,830 maximum contribution base. Tax is the 2026–27 resident scale with the full tax-free threshold. Medicare uses the 2025–26 single reduction thresholds because the 2026–27 reduction thresholds were not confirmed here. HELP, the Medicare levy surcharge, and salary packaging are not deducted. This is an estimate, not a determination of your pay or tax.

### Using the Timesheet on Our Home Page

Our [the timesheet](/) is the starting point. Enter your base hourly rate. If you are casual, tick the loading box – do not add loading to your rate. The calculator then shows annual gross, fortnightly and weekly amounts, estimated tax, Medicare, and super. You can adjust hours per week if you work part-time or irregular hours.

### Comparing Salaries and Job Offers

When you receive a salary offer, use the calculator to see what that equates to per hour. Conversely, if you know your hourly rate, see what it means as an annual package. Remember that super is additional – a $70,000 salary plus 12% super means your total employment cost is $78,400. Our [job pay](/topics/job-pay) page has more on comparing offers.

### Casual Loading and Award Rates

Casual employees are entitled to a 25% loading on top of the base rate. The calculator applies this automatically when you check the box. Award rates often specify a base hourly rate for permanent employees; casual loading is added. Check your award using our [casual loading](/topics/casual-loading) guide.

### Superannuation and Salary Packaging

Super guarantee is 12% of ordinary time earnings, paid by your employer. It does not reduce your take-home pay. If you salary sacrifice, your taxable income is lower, but the calculator does not model that. See our [super and packaging](/topics/super-and-packaging) page for details.

### Average Pay vs Your Pay

The ABS figures are averages, not medians for your specific job. For instance, full-time adult ordinary-time earnings of $2,083.70 per week is an average across all industries and states. Your pay may be higher or lower depending on your occupation, experience, and location. Our [average pay](/topics/average-pay) page explains how to interpret these numbers.

### Final Thoughts

Our salary after tax calculator is a practical tool for quick conversions. Always verify with your employer or a tax professional for precise figures. Use the [minimum wage](/topics/minimum-wage) page to ensure you are paid at least the legal minimum. The calculator is updated with the latest Fair Work and ATO rates.
